readings.title: Cooling a crowded bus stop
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A city wanted to add shade at a bus stop used by hospital visitors. A standard roof covered the bench but not the queue. The main obstacle was shade missing where passengers actually waited. People stood beyond the bench during busy periods and were exposed to direct afternoon sun. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used heat observations at bus arrival times. The team marked where queues formed and compared shade at different hours without interfering with passengers. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated the queue shifted as the sun moved. A fixed bench canopy would help some users but leave many standing in the hottest part of the pavement. The group then introduced a wider roof with a clear walking lane. Designers extended shade toward the queue while preserving space for pedestrians and people using wheelchairs. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: climate measures must follow daily movement. The best place for shade was determined by where people waited, not simply by the location of a bench. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in cooling a crowded bus stop, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: Rain warnings for basement shops
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Shopkeepers in a low street received a general storm alert. Several basement businesses did not realise that water could enter their storage rooms. The main obstacle was general warnings without local instructions. The alert described rainfall but offered no practical steps for owners with entrances below street level. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a review of past flooding accounts. The town compared reports from shopkeepers with drainage records and asked which preparations could be made in advance. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated water entered through two shared doorways. Small steps at those entrances could reduce losses even when the town could not prevent every storm. The group then introduced specific alerts and an entrance checklist. Future messages named affected streets and linked to simple instructions for moving goods and protecting electrical equipment. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: warnings should connect risk to action. People could respond more quickly when the message explained what the danger meant for their own premises. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in rain warnings for basement shops, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Trees after a dry summer
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A volunteer group planted young street trees before a long dry spell. Many residents offered to water them, but some trees still weakened. The main obstacle was watering effort that varied between sites. Different containers held different amounts, and volunteers could not tell which trees had already been visited. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a shared watering record. The group marked visits by date and agreed on simple amounts with advice from qualified maintenance staff. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated a few sites were repeatedly missed. The problem was uneven coordination rather than a lack of volunteers willing to help. The group then introduced paired routes and clear responsibility. Neighbours took short routes in pairs and reported damage or blocked tree pits to the council. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: community care needs a consistent method. Good intentions protected more trees when people could see what had been done and what remained. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in trees after a dry summer, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A cool room during heat alerts
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A community centre opened an air-conditioned room during heat alerts. The first notice was online, but many older residents did not see it. The main obstacle was information failing to reach likely visitors. Some people without regular internet access learned about the room only after the hottest hours had passed. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used calls through existing local networks. Staff asked health visitors, shopkeepers and neighbours which channels people already trusted for urgent information. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated printed notices and phone calls reached more people. The room became easier to find when opening times appeared at familiar places and could be confirmed by telephone. The group then introduced several channels with a single current schedule. The centre updated one source of truth and distributed matching information online, in print and by phone. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: access depends on communication as well as facilities. A safe place is useful only if those who need it know when and how to reach it. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a cool room during heat alerts, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful plan for urban climate adaptation must take account of the people who will use it. An idea may look complete on paper and still create difficulties during an ordinary week. Organizers therefore tried the city climate response programme on a small scale and invited comments from users with different schedules. They recorded benefits as well as the time and resources needed to provide them. Some findings supported the original aim, while others suggested that the method should change. The group published both kinds of result instead of presenting the trial as a simple success or failure. This allowed residents to discuss the next step with a clearer understanding of its possible effects.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 关于城市气候适应的有用方案必须考虑实际使用它的人。一个想法在纸上看似完整，平常使用时却仍可能出现困难。因此，组织者小规模试行该服务，并邀请时间安排不同的使用者提出意见。他们既记录益处，也记录提供这些益处所需的时间和资源。有些发现支持最初目标，另一些则表明方法应当调整。团队同时公布两类结果，而没有把试行简单说成成功或失败。这让居民能更清楚地了解可能的影响，再讨论下一步。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the climate response office about a community activity related to urban climate adaptation. Explain how different people can participate, what should be recorded, and how the results should be shared.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the city climate response programme. People have noticed shade missing where passengers actually waited, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
